field_commentary.value: 西行の庵は多数知られているが、小倉に庵があったことは、『山家集』に「小倉の麓に住みけるに鹿の鳴きけるを聞きて」の詞書（436番歌）や、「我がものと/秋の梢を思うかな/小倉の里に/家居せしより」（486番歌）とあることより推定され、現在、小倉山二尊院に西行法師庵跡の石碑がある。しかし、この能の舞台は、京都西方一帯の山を意味する「西山」にある西行の安室としか書かれていない。西山のどこかにあった西行の庵から見える小倉山の桜を描写したものかもしれない。

field_commentary_eng.value: There are several huts of Saigyō (Saigyō an) known. The one in Ogura is conjectured on the basis of the preface to poem no. 436 in Saigyō’s Sankashū “When he was living on the peak of Ogura he heard deer bellowing” and poem no. 486 “I think of the tree tops in autumn as my own since I have come to live in the village of Ogura”. Today, there is a stone monument in Nison temple at Ogura yama on the place Saigyō’s hut is supposed to have stood. However, the scene of this nō piece is just given as the quite hut of Saigyō in "Nishi yama" which refers to the mountains in the west of Kyōto in general. Perhaps it is the image of the cherry blossoms at Ogura yama seen from the hut of Saigyō situated somewhere in the mountains in the west.

field_scene_description_eng.value: An old man with white hair (shite, in reality the spirit of the cherry trees) appears in front of the monk Saigyō (waki) who is known for having composed a poem putting the blame for people gathering for hanami on the cherry blossoms. The old man explains that sin can only be attributed to beings with emotions, and the gatherings are not the fault of the cherry blossoms that are devoid of emotions. While he sings of the famous site for cherry blossoms and performs a dance, it begins to dawn. The spirit of the cherry blossoms is deploring the end of hanami as there are only the night blossoms left on Ogura yama shining white.

field_scene_description_eng.value: An old man (shite, in reality, the deity of the Matsunoo shrine) and another man (tsure) are explaining the history of the Matsunoo shrine to a retainer (waki) who happens to be visiting. On the surface of the river (Katsura gawa) flowing by the shrine fallen leaves are floating like colorful brocade, autumn leaves that came down from Ogura yama. While their color changes day by day, they are compared with the evergreen treetops on Matsunoo yama in the precincts of the shrine.

field_commentary_eng.value: The Yōkyoku taikan comments that Ogura yama is compared here to Aone ga mine, but as Ogura yama is a famous site for autumn leaves, green (ao) does not match. Furthermore, Ogura yama is not east from Arashi yama but in the north which again is a contradiction. The “color of the pines” (matsu) refers obviously to Matsunoo shrine. Ogura yama is cited probably for its image as a famous place for autumn leaves.

field_commentary_eng.value:
A description of the scenery around Sagano. It may be based on the poem in the Shinkokinshū which reads:

 

“Ogura Mountain

at its foot flowering plume 

grass blankets the fields

spearheads dimly visible

this dusky autumn evening”

 

(Shinkokinshū, chapter ‘Autumn 1’, poem no. 347; English translation by Rodd, Laurel R. (2015): p.152)

There they meet a mad woman called Hyakuman (shite). The child says that this mad woman must be the mother from whom he was separated, and as the person from Yoshino talks to her, she tells them how she arrived at Seiryō-ji Temple from Nara in search of her child.

field_commentary.value: 曲舞の前半は、中大兄皇子（後の天智天皇）が、奈良の吉野山から、須磨・明石を経て、九州筑前の朝倉に至り、宮殿（木の丸殿）を作ったことを謡う。百済救済のため九州に宮を作るったのは史実だが、その前に須磨明石に三年を過ごしたことの典拠未詳。吉野から九州に向かう途中にある著名な歌枕であることと、『源氏物語』で光源氏が須磨・明石で三年を過ごした地という文学的ニュアンスが、「徒に過ごす」の連想で用いられたか。

field_commentary_eng.value:
Sugimura Danjō no Shōhitsu, in order to announce his real name, recites the poem by Emperor Tenji that refers to "calling out one's name": "As I am at Ki no Marodono Palace in Asakura,
A child walks by, calling out their name—Whose child might it be?" ( Shin Kokin Wakashū #168) In doing so, he references Emperor Tenji’s time spent secluded in the village of Asakura in Tsukushi. The "Ki no Marodono" refers to the simple wooden residence which was built to serve as an imperial residence during Emperor Tenji's military expedition to Baekje (on the Korean Peninsula) in Asakura, Kyushu. This poem was composed by Emperor Tenji, then Crown Prince, while in mourning for his mother, Empress Saimei. In the poem, he reflects on his time at Ki no Marodono in Asakura, wondering whose child might be passing by, calling out their name.

field_scene_description.value: 杉村弾正(シテ)は、紀州粉川寺にて、人を泊めてはいけない日に宿を所望し断られる。しかし、稚児梅夜叉(子方)の機転で、仮名字（偽名）を名乗って宿を得る。後日、梅夜叉に会うために再び寺を訪れたところ、寺の住職（ワキ）に、本当の名前を尋ねられたので、仮名字に関する曲舞を舞った後に答えようと言い、曲舞〔くせまい〕を謡う場面。

field_scene_description_eng.value:
On a day when people are not allowed to stay overnight at Kokawa-ji Temple in Kii province, Sugimura Danjō (shite) asks for lodging but is refused. However, with the help of the young boy Umeyasha (kokata), he is able to obtain accommodation under a false name. Later, when he visits the temple again to see Umeyasha, the temple priest (waki) asks him about his real name, Danjō tells him that he will answer him after he has danced (and sung) a Kusemai about his pseudonym. In this scene he sings the Kusemai.

On a day when people are not allowed to stay overnight at Kokawa-ji Temple in Kii province, Sugimura Danjō (shite) asks for lodging but is refused. However, with the help of the young boy Umeyasha (kokata), he is able to obtain accommodation under a false name. Later, when he visits the temple again to see Umeyasha, the temple priest (waki) asks him about his real name, Danjō tells him that he will answer him after he has danced (and sung) a Kusemai about his pseudonym. In this scene he sings the Kusemai.

field_commentary.value: 秀吉は、織田信長の命で備中高松城の毛利氏を攻めていたが、明智光秀の謀反を知り、急ぎ毛利と和睦をむすんで、明智討伐のため京都に向う。その道中に通過した地名が詠み込まれる最初が「明石潟」。「五更」は、午前3時～4時頃なので、「夜が明ける」と掛詞で、秀吉が夜を徹して駆けつけたことが表現される。本曲は豊臣秀吉が自身の功績を能に作らせた豊公能のひとつで、文禄三年（1594）には成立。

field_commentary_eng.value: Hideyoshi had been attacking the Mōri clan at Takamatsu Castle, in Bitchū on the orders of Oda Nobunaga, but when he learned of Akechi Mitsuhide's rebellion, he hastily made peace with the Mōri clan and headed for Kyōto to defeat Mitsuhide. The first poem to include the names of the places he passed along the way was the poem “Akashi gata” (Akashi Lagoon). Gokō is the time around 3:00 to 4:00 a.m., so the poem is called "Yoru ga akeru" (Dawn is breaking), expressing Hideyoshi's rush through the night. This piece is one of the so called Hōkōnō in which Toyotomi Hideyoshi had his own achievements made into Nō plays, completed in the year 1594.

Akashi is the place where Hikaru Genji moved after he was exiled to Suma, and where he continued to live in loneliness. Is there, in accordance with this story line, an additional image of Akashi as a lonely place where people could not talk about their dreams?

In this context, Akashi is also the name of a volume of The Tale of Genji, as the chapter name is deliberately integrated in the text.

field_commentary_eng.value:
In a context of continuing to think that one’s life will last as long as a thread, even though there is no point in living that long, the word “omoi akasu” (to reveal) and the place name “Akashi” are used as kakekotoba (a wordplay using homophonic words), while also borrowing from a poem by Fujiwara no Kintsune and recalling the words "chidori" (plover) and "naku" (cry/sing): 

 "in anguished yearning

I await break of day at

Akashi Bay plovers

on the waves crying out I

weep on a tear-drenched pillow" 

 

(Shinkokinshū, Vol. 14, ’Koi uta 4 -Love poems 4’ , poem no. 1331; English translation by Rodd, Laurel R. (2015): p.547)

field_scene_description.value: 牛若（子方）が渡された笛の由来を、母の常磐（シテ）に尋ねる場面。常盤は、今となっては隠すこともないといって、笛の蝉の部分に巻いている錦の布を解いて、虫食の跡を見せる。虫食いは、300年の時を経て弘法大師の手に渡り、源氏の棟梁源義朝の末子牛若の手に渡るだろうと読める。

field_scene_description_eng.value: In this scene, Ushiwaka (kokata) asks his mother, Tokiwa (shite), about the origin of the flute he inherited. Saying that there was nothing to hide now, Tokiwa unravelled the brocade cloth wrapped around the semi (a cut out piece of wood in form of a cicada) of the flute to show the traces of insect damage. It can be read that over the course of 300 years the remains of this flute were passed on through the hands of Kōbō Daishi (the Buddhist monk Kūkai) to Ushiwaka, the youngest son of Minamoto no Yoshitomo, the leader of the Minamoto clan.

field_commentary.value: ここでの明石は、古歌や物語によって形成されたイメージは影響しない。四天王寺から見える風景。なお、現在の四天王寺からこの風景は見ることができない。当時は四天王寺の目前に難波海が面しており、住吉神社を含め、太陽が沈む海面を広く見渡すことができたが、現在は埋め立てられている。日想観（じっそうがん）は、極楽浄土の方向（西）を心から認識するために、西に沈む夕日を観るという修行で、平安時代ごろから貴賤僧俗を問わずされた。特に、四天王寺の石の鳥居は、正しく西の方向に建っているので、鳥居を通して西に沈む夕日を観るために多くの人々が集った。

field_commentary_eng.value: The image of Akashi here is not affected by the images formed by ancient poems and stories but we are presented the view from Shitennō-ji Temple, although this scenery cannot be seen from the present day Shitennō-ji Temple. At that time, the Naniwa sea was right in front of the Shitennō-ji Temple, and one could survey large parts of the sea, where the sun was setting, including Sumiyoshi Shrine. Today the coast is banked up. The jissōkan is the practice of watching the sun set in the west in order to become sincerely aware of the direction of the Pure Land (west), and it was practiced since the Heian period by people of high or low birth, layman or Buddhist monk. In particular, the stone torii gate of Shitennō-ji Temple stands in direction to the west. Many people gathered at this torii to watch the sun set in the west.

field_scene_description.value: 盲目の乞食である弱法師（シテ）が四天王寺で出逢った、高安左衛門通俊（ワキ、実は弱法師の父）に、日想観を勧められ、盲目になる前に見えていた、難波江の風景を描写する場面。月が照り輝き、さわやかな風のなか、住吉神社の松原を通して難波の海面に月が映るのがみえ、太陽が沈もうとしている。右手には、淡路島、絵島といった島々が見え、さらにその向こうに、須磨の浦、明石の浦も見える。左手には紀の海と、パノラマの風景が弱法師の心の目に広がる。

field_scene_description_eng.value: In this scene, a blind beggar named Yoroboshi (shite) meets Takayasu Saemon Michitoshi (waki, in reality Yoroboshi’s father) at Shitennō-ji Temple, he encourages him to do the jissōkan (the first of the sixteen stages to be reborn in the western paradise). Yoroboshi than describes the scenery of Naniwa bay, which he could see before he became blind. The moon is shining, the breeze is fresh, through the pine grove of Sumiyoshi Shrine one can see the reflection of the moon on the surface of the sea at Naniwa, and the sun is about to set. To the right, the islands of Awaji and Eshima can be seen, and beyond them, Suma no ura and Akashi no ura. To the left, the sea of Ki  ̶  a panoramic scenery takes shape in the mind's eye of Yoroboshi.

field_commentary.value: ここでの明石は、『源氏物語』の巻名の「明石」を意味する。供養の対象となる名前を読み上げる仏教法要の作法による。文脈上は、光源氏が都を追われ配流の地・須磨を出て、明石に移り、苦しみに身を尽くしていた（苦しみから抜け出せずにいた）という物語の筋を説明するとともに、そのような苦しみから早く抜け出すべきで、仏教的修行によって四つの智慧が全く明らかな状態（＝四智円明）になって、極楽浄土に行くことを願うべき、という主張を重ねる。語法としては、「明らか」から「明石」が導かれる。

field_commentary_eng.value: Akashi here refers to the name of the chapter "Akashi" in The Tale of Genji. The name of the person to be honoured is read out in a Buddhist memorial service. While it explains the plot when Hikaru Genji was forced to leave the capital, left his exile in Suma and moved to Akashi, where he was immersed in suffering (and was unable to escape it), the play conveys the view, that such sufferings should be dissolved quickly, and one should hope to go to the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss by becoming completely clear about the four wisdoms through Buddhist practice (= shichi enmyō). From the expression "akiraka” the word “Akashi” is associated.

field_scene_description_eng.value: The spirit of Murasaki Shikibu (shite) appears while Agoi no hōin (waki) (hōin is a rank of a monk) is visiting the Ishiyama Temple and asks him to make a memorial service for The Tale of Genji. As the Hōin begins the memorial service, the spirit of Murasaki Shikibu appears again, and in lieu of an offering for the memorial service, she dances while reading out a prayer (a text describing the wishes to the gods and Buddha). Here, the content of the wish, as it revolves around the uncovering of the Buddhist teaching, is that The Tale of Genji will make her become a Buddha.

field_commentary_eng.value: The scene is not a description of the scenery of Akashi no ura but rather a stylistic device. The village woman is actually not the daughter of an ama (fisher) who lives in Akashi no ura.  "Akashi no ura ni" is a kakekotoba (a wordplay with homophonic words) with “(na o) nan to akasan” (to reveal one’s name). Akashi no ura is associated with “ama no ko” (ama child), suggesting that the village woman is a person who does not have a fixed abode, implying that she is a butterfly spirit who flies from flower to flower.

The woman replies that she does not need to tell him what her name is and that she is like a poor fisherman's child who has no permanent home.

field_commentary.value: 柿本人麻呂は平安時代より歌聖として敬われ、鎌倉時代には歌合の場に御影を掲げる習慣になった。本曲でもこの前の謡に「人丸赤人の御影を掛け」と説明されている。御歌合を始める前に人麻呂の和歌を詠みあげる場面なので、実際に目前にある明石の浦の風景を描写しているわけではない。ただし、和歌に詠まれている明石の浦の島々と朝霧に見え隠れする舟の情景から、舟と似た形の月（三日月）が淡く雲間に見え隠れする情景を連想し、明石の浦から見える淡路島を導く。淡路島は、国生み神話で最初に誕生した天地開闢の島なので、続く「はじめて歌の遊び」の語を導く。歌合の始まりをも導いているか。

field_commentary_eng.value: Kakinomoto no Hitomaro was revered as a great poet from the Heian period (794-1185) onwards. In the Kamakura period (1185-1333) it became customary to display his image (and that of Yamabe no Akahito) at poetry festivals. In this piece, too, the previous Nō-chant is described as “Hitomaro Akahito no miei o kake” ("hanging up the image of Hitomaro and Akahito"). As this is the scene in which Hitomaro's waka poem is recited before starting the poetry contest, it does not actually describe the scenery of Akashi no ura directly. However, the scene of the islands of Akashi no ura and the boat hidden in the morning mist in the waka poem reminds us of the moon (crescent moon), which has a similar shape to the boat, hiding in the clouds, and takes us to Awaji Island, which can be seen from Akashi no ura. Awaji Island is the island of the creation of heaven and earth (tenchi kaibyaku) in the myth of the birth of the nation (kuniumi no shinwa), which leads to the words “hajimete uta no asobi'”. Does this also refer to the beginning of the poetry contest?

field_scene_description_eng.value:
To start the poetry contest in front of the Emperor, someone first recites a waka poem by Kakinomoto no Hitomaro, which reads as follows:

 

“dimly through morning

mist over Akashi Bay my

longings trace the ship

vanishing from sight floating

silently behind the isle”

 

 (Kokinshū, vol. 9, chapter ‘Kiryo - Travel poems’, poem no. 409; english translation by Rodd, Laurel R. (1984): p.165), and while admiring the scene and atmosphere depicted by the poem, they are waiting for the Emperor to announce the start of the contest. Ki no Tsurayuki is a real-life poet and appears in this Nō play as the judge.

field_commentary_eng.value:
“noboreba kudaru ya inabune no” (“as the rice boats pole upstream and back….”) refers to a poem in the Kokinshū 

 

As the rice boats ply

the Mogami River they

pole upstream and back  ̶

you too should come again it`s

only this month I say “no”

 

(Kokinshū, Vol. 20, chapter `Ayuma uta - Eastern Songs`, no. 1092; English translation by Rodd, Laurel R.  (1984): p.372), and “honobono to Akashi no ura” (“dimly Akashi Bay…”) refers to Kakinomoto no Hitomaro`s poem 

 

“dimly through morning

mist over Akashi Bay my

longings trace the ship

vanishing from sight floating

silently behind the isle”

 

 (Kokinshū, vol. 9, chapter ‘Kiryo - Travel poems’, poem no. 409; English translation by Rodd, Laurel R. (1984): p.165). In particular, Kakinomoto no Hitomaro's poem "honobono to" evokes the image of “Akashi no ura” in connection with  “leaving ships” and a “sad farewell”.

field_commentary.value: 明石は光源氏が明石の上と契りを結んだ土地。「明石の浦」は歌枕で、「浦浪の」続けることで、浪の縁で「立ち帰る」の語を導き、明石の上の舟が帰ることなく留まっていることを表現する。ここでは、歌枕としての「明石」「明石の浦」よりも、『源氏物語』の「明石の巻」の物語の舞台としての地の意味の方が強いだろう。

field_commentary_eng.value: Akashi is the land where Hikaru Genji made a pledge to Akashi no Ue. “Akashi no ura" is an utamakura, and uranami no, which implies the “coming and going” of the waves, refers to the fact that Akashi no Ue's boat stays there without returning. Here, the meaning of the place as a setting for the story of the chapter Akashi (Akashi no maki) in The Tale of Genji is probably stronger than that of "Akashi" or "Akashi no ura" as utamakura.

field_scene_description.value: 明石の上と光源氏の再会の場面。住吉詣に来た光源氏は、かつて過ごした明石の浦の方から来た舟が帰るようでもなく、しかも舟陰に誰かが隠れ忍んでいるようなのを不思議に思い、声をかける。明石の上（シテ）は、「誰か？などと、よそよそしく尋ねるのは、別れた時に琴の緒が変わらないうちに再会しようと約束したことは、もう住吉の岸に生える草のように忘れたのですか」と返事をする。住吉の岸に生える草とは忘れ草のこと。ロンギは地謡が謡うが光源氏の言葉の代弁である。

field_scene_description_eng.value: In this scene Akashi no Ue and Hikaru Genji reunite. Hikaru Genji, who came to Sumiyoshi on a pilgrimage, wonders why a boat from Akashi no ura, where he once spent time, does not seem to be returning, and why someone seems to be hiding behind the boat, he goes there to ask about it. Akashi no Ue (shite) replies, "`Who is it?’ To ask this distantly... Have you forgotten, like the grass that grows on the shore of Sumiyoshi, that when we parted, we promised to meet again before the Koto cord changed?” The grass that grows on the shore of Sumiyoshi is the "wasuregusa" (orange daylily, Hemerocallis fulva). Even though the rongi is chanted by a Nō-chorus, it reflects Hikaru Genji's words.

field_commentary_eng.value: The scene in which Akashi no Ue's boat travels along the coast from Akashi to “the place where the moon rises= the east= Sumiyoshi Shrine” corresponds to the scenery associated with Akashi in utamakura, with boats pasing by. Akashi no Ue is the daughter of the Buddhist monk Akashi, who lives in Akashi. When Hikaru Genji, who had been living a lonely life in Suma after being forced to leave the capital, moved to Akashi under the guidance of Sumiyoshi Shrine, Akashi no Ue became his lover in accordance with her father's wishes, but she felt reluctant because of their difference in status. Akashi has the image of a rural but elegant and fascinating place, which may be reflected in the character of Akashi no Ue.

field_commentary.value: 人丸（=柿本人麻呂）が明石を詠った歌「ほのほのと / 明石の浦の / あさ霧に / 島かくれゆく / 舟をしそ思ふ」（『古今集』・巻第九・羇旅・409番歌）を引用している。この歌は『古今集仮名序』で人丸の代表歌のひとつとして挙げられ、馴染みのある歌のためか、能では頻繁に引用される。合戦中、須磨の浦で旅寝をしていた平忠度が、明け方の明石の浦の光景を目前にし、480年程昔に柿本人麻呂が、明石の浦を行きかう舟を眺めて詠んだ心境に共感する。人麻呂の心境は、舟に乗っている人との惜別の念だが、忠度の場合はこの世との惜別だろう。「明石」「舟」によって別れの情念を喚起させる型が成立しているか。

field_commentary_eng.value:
The poem quotes Hitomaru's (Kakinomoto no Hitomaro) poem about Akashi, 

 

“dimly through morning

mist over Akashi Bay my

longings trace the ship

vanishing from sight floating

silently behind the isle”

 

 (Kokinshū, vol. 9, chapter ‘Kiryo - Travel poems’, poem no. 409; English translation by Rodd, Laurel R. (1984): p.165). This poem is listed as one of Hitomaru's representative poems in the "Kokinshū kana-jo" (the Kana preface of the Kokinwakashū) and is frequently quoted in Nō plays, probably because it is familiar to the audience. Taira no Tadanori, who on his journey was staying over night in Suma no ura during the ongoing war, saw the scene of Akashi no ura at dawn and sympathised with the feelings of Kakinomoto no Hitomaro, who wrote the poem about 480 years ago when he watched the boats passing by Akashi no ura. While Hitomaro is feeling like parting from the people on the boat, Tadanoris is feeling like parting from the world. The words "Akashi" and "boat" evoke the sentiment of parting.

field_scene_description.value: 歌人である藤原俊成（ツレ）の前に、平忠度の霊（シテ）が現れ、一の谷の合戦で岡部の六弥太（ワキ）に殺された時、身につけていた短冊の和歌を、俊成が『千載集』に収めてくれたが、「読み人知らず」と作者名を秘したことが心残りだと訴える。俊成は、忠度は朝敵なので名前を明記できなかったが、すばらしい和歌なので、忠度の名誉は語り継がれるだろうと慰める。この場面は、和歌が永く人々に伝えられている例を語り合う場面で、三十一字の和歌を初めて詠んだ素戔嗚尊の例のあと、忠度の霊が生前に須磨の浦で旅寝をしたとき、目前の景色を眺めながら、昔、人丸（=柿本人麻呂）が「明石の浦の朝霧」の歌を歌った趣きに思いをはせたことを思い出したところ。

field_scene_description_eng.value:
The spirit of Taira no Tadanori (shite) appears to the poet Fujiwara no Toshinari (tsure) and complains that the poem he had with him when he was killed by Okabe no Rokuyata (waki) at the battle of Ichinotani, was included in the Senzai wakashū by Toshinari but sadly the name of the author was concealed by the term “Poet unknown”. Toshinari consoles him by saying that he could not specify the author's name because Tadanori was an enemy of the imperial court, but that the poem was so wonderful that his honour would be passed on.

This scene is a discussion of waka poems that have been handed down for a long time. After the example of Susanoo-no-Mikoto, who was the first  to compose a 31-character waka poem, the spirit of Tadanori recalls that when he slept on a journey at Suma no ura before his death, he looked at the scenery in front of him and thought about the atmosphere of the poem "Akashi no ura no asagiri" (The morning mist in Akashi Bay) that Hitomaru (Kakinomoto no Hitomaro) had composed long ago.

field_commentary.value: 平家が布陣した一の谷の城は、前には海、後ろには山を控えた堅固な要塞だが、左には須磨、右には明石があり双方から船や千鳥が行きかう風雅な土地でもあると説明される。須磨とともに言及する点や、行き交う船を詠み込む点は、歌枕としての明石のイメージを踏襲している。「とよりかくより」は「あちらからもこちらからも」の意だが、「と」は、「明石の門」を掛ける。千鳥は須磨から連想されるイメージである。

field_commentary_eng.value: The castle at Ichinotani, where the Heike were stationed, is described as a solid fortress with the sea in front and the mountains behind it, but also as an elegant place with Suma on the left and Akashi on the right, where ships and plovers come and go. The reference to Suma and the passing ships corresponds with the image of Akashi as a utamakura (famous place with a poetic association).  “to yori kaku yori” implies “from here and there” und “to” represents “Akashi no to" (Akashi strait). The plover is an image associated with Suma.

field_commentary_eng.value: Waka no ura is used as a poetic device. The word moshiogusa (seaweed), which is associated with Waka no ura,  expresses that like the seeweed which is washed by the waves of the sea the book (copy of the Man'yōshū) is washed. When drenched, the fresh ink on the paper is dissolved, revealing the plot of Kuronushi.

field_commentary_eng.value: In the Kokinshū kana-jo, the commentary about the poet Ōtomo no Kuronushi is as follows: "Ōtomo no Kuronushi’s songs are rustic in form; they are like a mountaineer with a bundle of firewood on his back resting in the shade of the blossoms" (English translation by Rodd, Laurel R. (1984): p.46). The  appearance of the shite is in accordance with this description. “Waka no ura" here is used as a poetic device in waka poems. The waka poem by Taira no Yoshinao, "Everything is in vain, the drying seaweed in the bay of Waka, the time before it was laid down, I want to remember that” (Shokugoshūi wakashū, vol. 16, poem no. 1083) refers to the well known context of the preface to the Kokinwakashū where Ōtomo no Kuronushi is mentioned as having written waka poems with great enthusiasm even in his old age.

field_commentary_eng.value:
On the way from Sagano to Shikimigahara there lies Ogura, a famous place, which is mentioned as a transit point. Shikimigahara is a field at the western foot of Atago-yama and used as utamakura (a famous place with a poetic association). It is mentioned in Horikawa hyakushu (Hundred Poems during the reign of Emperor Horikawa) in the section winter poems:

“Even though rain in winter keeps drizzling for days, the colour of Atago-yama and Shikimigahara doesn’t change” (by Fujiwara no Akinaka)

The former name of the area was Kazurano-gun Saga Machibara.

field_commentary.value: 鼓の滝近辺の歌枕を挙げながら、春の情景を描写している。鼓の滝は有馬山の名所で、桜の名所として平安時代から知られていた。シテの木こりが、この場所で長く過ごしている理由を説明するとき、鼓の滝の花（桜）があまりにすばらしいので、名残を惜しむ気持ちがあるためだと言う、「あり」と、「ありまやま」を掛けて、有馬山の鼓の滝と続けている。なお現在、有馬温泉近くに、鼓ヶ滝公園があり滝が流れる。そのほとりには有明桜の碑がたてられているが、かつて二本だったという有明桜そのものは今はない。

field_commentary_eng.value: By introducing the utamakura Tsuzumi no taki and its surroundings the scene evokes a spring landscape. Tsuzumi no taki is a famous place on Mount Arima, known for its cherry blossoms since the Heian period. When the woodcutter (shite) explains why he has spent so much time here, he says that the flowers (cherry blossoms) at Tsuzumi no taki are so wonderful that he regrets he has to part. The word “ari” in the sentence “hana ni nagori wa ari (mayama)” is a pivot word for “arimayama”, the sentence continuing with “arimayama no tsuzumi no taki” (Tsuzumi no taki of Arima Mountain).  Today, in the vicinity of Arima Onsen lies the Tsuzumi-ga-taki Park with this waterfall. Although there is a stele for the Ariake cherry trees near the waterfall, the two cherry trees that are said to have once stood there are no longer.

僧（ワキ、ワキツレ）が都から芦屋へ向かう道中を謡った道行。能《忠度》の冒頭のワキ僧によるサシ「城南の離宮に赴き」から「鳴尾潟」までをそのまま借用しているので、意味は「有馬山」の《忠度》参照のこと。

ただし、《忠度》の最終目的地は須磨だが、本曲では芦屋なので、芦屋到着の謡で締める。本曲のワキ僧は本当の旅僧ではなく、執権の最明寺時頼の仮の姿であるため、心からの心象ではない。借用された謡であることは理にかなっているかもしれない。

field_commentary_eng.value: This is a michiyuki passage in the play mentioning the places some monks (waki, wakizure) pass by on their way from the capital to Ashiya.  It cites exactly the opening chant of the monk (waki) in the Nō Tadanori beginning with "sashi:  Jōnan no rikyū ni omomuki…” and ending with “Naruo gata”. (Please see for Tadanori.) The citation ends however, as the monks in the play are heading for Ashiya instead of Suma as in Tadanori. As the monk (waki) in this piece is not really a traveling monk but rather the regent Saimyōji Tokiyori in disguise, the content of the chant (hardship, floating world) does not reflect his actual feelings. We may interpret it as a borrowed chant.

field_scene_description.value:
能《藤栄》の冒頭。諸国一見の修行中の僧が、都から芦屋に向かう道中。通った歌枕を読み込んだ謡を謡って、旅をしていることを表す「道行」の場面。

ワキ僧は実は、鎌倉幕府執権の最明寺時頼（北条時頼）で、身分を僧といつわり諸国を巡見している。到着した芦屋で、領主の子月若が、叔父の藤栄に領地を横領されたことを知り、藤栄を懲らしめる。

field_scene_description_eng.value:
It is the opening scene of the Nō piece Tōei. It is about a monk who is touring the country and doing ascetic practice (shokoku ikken) and is currently on his way from the capital to Ashiya.

The michiyuki scene is expressed through a Nō chant in which the utamakura on their way are recited to indicate that the monk is on a journey.

The monk (waki) is actually Saimyōji Tokiyori (Hōjō Tokiyori), a regent of the Kamakura shogunate, disguised as a monk to travel the country. When he arrives in Ashiya, he learns that the former feudal lord’s son named Tsukiwaka has had his territory usurped by his uncle Tōei. He now goes to punish Tōei.

field_commentary.value: 僧（ワキ、ワキツレ）は「世を捨て人」つまり出家の身なので、道のりの地名によって、憂うことが多い浮き世での思い出が喚起されながら通り過ぎている。「有馬山」は摂津国有馬郡の山で、歌枕。「昆陽の池」から北西の方向にある。「憂き事の捨つる身までもあり（世を捨てた身でも憂き事はある）」の「あり」と「有馬山」の「あり」が掛詞になっている。そして、「有馬山隠れかねたる（山のように隠れがたい）」と続けて、僧になっても浮世のつらさから離れることができない、つまり忘れることができないのかと落胆しているのである。

field_commentary_eng.value: Since the monks (waki, wakitsure) are “people who have renounced the world” i.e. entered priesthood, the names of the places they pass along the way reminds them of the floating world with its many hardships. Arimayama is a mountain in Arima County, Settsu Province. It is a utamakura and is located in the northwestern direction of Koya no ike. The word “ari (exist)” in the sentence “ukikoto no sutsuru mi made mo ari” (Even those who have renounced the world lament) is a kakekotoba (a wordplay using homophonic words) to “ari” in “Arimayama”. The scene continues with “Arimayama kakurekanetaru” (As hard as it is for a mountain to hide from the world, so it is for me), which expresses his dismay that even after becoming a monk, he is unable to part from the sorrows of the floating world (i.e. he cannot forget).

field_scene_description_eng.value:
It is the opening scene of the Nō piece Tadanori. 

A monk (waki) who was a vassal of Fujiwara no Toshinari (Shunzei) and took the tonsure after Toshinari's death heads with his fellow monks (wakitsure) from the capital to the western provinces.

The michiyuki scene (the enumeration of place names and landscapes in Japanese literature, performing arts and music that illustrates a person's journey) is performed through a Nō chant reciting the utamakura on their way from the capital to Suma no ura in order to illustrate that they are on a journey. After this scene, the monks meet the spirit of Tadanori in Suma no ura.

field_commentary.value: シテの漁翁は、夕浪が引いて夜となり、また朝になると言って、朝に掛けて「朝倉」を導く。そして「朝倉や。木の丸殿にあらばこそ」と天智天皇の歌「朝倉やきのまろどのにわがをれば名のりをしつつ行くはたが子ぞ」（『新古今集』168番）を想起させる回答をする。「きのまろどの」は百済出兵のために九州朝倉に仮に作られた木づくりの質素な天皇の住まい。『新古今集』168番の和歌は、母・斉明天皇の喪に服している皇太子時代の天智天皇の歌で、朝倉にある木の丸御殿にいると、名前を名乗っていく子がいるが、あれは誰の子どもなのだ？という意味。質素な宮殿での警備のために通る人には必ず名乗らせていたという伝承がある（『十訓抄』）。この歌の「名のりをしつつ」の引用から、漁翁は「名のりをしても行かまし」と言う。つまり、「もしここが朝倉にある木の丸殿であるなら必ず名のりをするが、今は名のならずにおこう」と我が身を明かさず、はぐらかす。朝倉は「名を明かす」を導く地名で、もし今朝倉にいるなら我が名を名乗るが、漁翁がいる場所は朝倉ではないので名前は明かさないのである。

field_commentary_eng.value:
The old fisherman as shite, uses the fact that the evening wave recedes into the night and returns back in the morning to play on the word "asa" (morning) and introduce the place name Asakura. He responds to the monk saying "Asakura! If only I were at Ki no Marodono", referring to the famous poem by Emperor Tenji (Shin Kokin Wakashū #168) that translates as: "As I am at Ki no Marodono Palace in Asakura,
A child walks by, calling out their name—
Whose child might it be?" "Ki no marodono" refers to the simple wooden residence which was built to serve as an imperial residence during Emperor Tenji's military expedition to Baekje (on the Korean Peninsula) in Asakura, Kyushu. The poem was written by Emperor Tenji while he was crown prince, mourning his mother, Empress Saimei, at Asakura. In the poem he expresses his curiosity towards the child passing by, wondering who they may be, as each person was required to announce their name when passing by the palace, a custom that is recorded in the Jikkinshō. Playing off the line in the poem “calling out one’s name”, the old fisherman responds, "If this were the Ki no Marudono at Asakura, I would indeed announce my name." In other words, he implies that if they were at Asakura, he would declare his name, but as they are not, he will leave his identity ambiguous and avoid revealing it. Although Asakura is a place that invites "declaring one's name," here, they are not in Asakura, so he refrains from doing so.

field_commentary.value: 杉村弾正少弼（シテ）は、天智天皇が筑紫朝倉の里に籠っていたことに触れ、「朝倉の里では人は必ずその名を名のるべし」という綸言の和歌「朝倉やきのまろどのにわがをれば名のりをしつつ行くはたが子ぞ」（『新古今集』168番）を天智天皇が詠んだことにちなみ、和歌浦がある紀伊国粉川においても本名を名のろうと言う。「きのまろどの」は百済出兵のために九州朝倉に仮に作られた木づくりの質素な天皇の住まい。『新古今集』168番歌は、母・斉明天皇の喪に服している皇太子時代の天智天皇の歌で、朝倉にある木の丸御殿にいると、名前を名乗っていく子がいるが、あれは誰の子どもなのだ？という意味。朝倉は「名を明かす」語を導く地名となっており、本曲の舞台は朝倉ではないが、和歌で名を明かすように命じたことから、和歌の浦と名のついたこの場所なので、和歌の言葉に裏はない（「和歌の浦波」をかける）、つまり和歌の言葉は絶対であり、名乗らないでおくことはできないと言う。

field_commentary_eng.value:
In his kusemai dance, Sugimura Danjō no Shōhitsu alludes to Emperor Tenji’s time in seclusion at the village of Asakura in Tsukushi and references the Jikkinshō "in Asakura, all must announce their name." He cites the poem by Emperor Tenji, "As I am at Ki no Marodono Palace in Asakura, a child walks by, calling out their name—Whose child might it be?" (Shin Kokin Wakashū #168)
Inspired by this precedent, Sugimura declares that he, too, will reveal his true name here in Kokawa, in Kii Province, where Wakanoura Bay lies.
The "Ki no Marodono" mentioned in the poem refers to the simple wooden residence which was built to serve as an imperial residence during Emperor Tenji's military expedition to Baekje (on the Korean Peninsula) in Asakura, Kyushu.  The poem was composed by Emperor Tenji, then Crown Prince, while in mourning for his mother, Empress Saimei. In the poem, he reflects on his time at Ki no Marodono in Asakura, wondering whose child might be passing by, calling out their name, as each person was required to announce their name when passing the palace. Asakura thus became a place associated with "revealing one’s name."
Though the setting of this story is not Asakura, Sugimura draws on the poem’s command to "reveal one’s name" to proclaim that, here at Wakanoura, which contains "waka" (Japanese poetry), he will honor the command of the poem. By a wordplay on "Wakanoura waves" (interpreted as the honesty of poetry), he implies that the words of poetry are absolute; therefore, he cannot remain without announcing his name.

field_scene_description.value: 杉村弾正少弼(シテ)は、紀州粉川寺にて、人を泊めてはいけない日に宿を所望し断られる。しかし、稚児梅夜叉(子方)の機転で、仮名字（偽名）を名乗って宿を得る。後日、梅夜叉に会うために再び寺を訪れたところ、寺の住職（ワキ）に、本当の名前を尋ねられたので、仮名字に関する曲舞を舞った後に答えようと言い、曲舞〔くせまい〕を謡う。曲舞のなかで、天智天皇が筑紫朝倉の里に籠っていたことに触れ、朝倉の里では、人は必ずその名を名のることになっていたというから、ここ粉河寺でも、自分も本名を名乗ろうと言う。

field_scene_description_eng.value:
Sugimura Danjō (the shite) arrives at Kokawadera Temple in Kii Province seeking accommodation but is refused, as it is a day when guests are not permitted. However, thanks to the cleverness of a page named Ume no Yasha (the kokata), he is allowed to stay under the assumed name. Later, when he revisits the temple to see Ume no Yasha again, the temple’s head priest (the waki) asks him for his true name. Sugimura replies that he will reveal his real name after performing a kusemai dance on the theme of assumed names, and then begins his dance.
During the kusemai, he references Emperor Tenji’s time in seclusion in the village of Asakura in Tsukushi, noting how, in Asakura, all were required to announce their names. Drawing a parallel, he declares that he too will now reveal his true name here at Kokawadera.

field_commentary.value: 「長柄」は「ながらへ」と同音を重ねる序の詞で、命を長らえる、生き続ける意味と掛けている。つらいこの世を生きるという意味の「憂き世を渡らんと」のいう謡の句は、橋の縁語である「渡る」に接続する。この世は無常であるという仏教思想のもと、この世にながらえることは、つらいものと考える。長柄の橋は、相次ぐ水難で何度架けても壊れてしまった歴史を持つ。いつまでこの橋はもつのだろうかという儚いイメージが形成され、儚い世をつらいながらも生きるというネガディブな感情と結びついている。

field_commentary_eng.value: The word Nagara (from Nagara no hashi) is linked to the homophone nagarae, meaning “to live on, to endure life,” serving as a poetic epitheton symbolizing the continuity of life. This is linked with the expression ukiyo wo wataran to, meaning “to cross through this sorrowful world,” which connects the verb wataru "to cross", commonly associated with bridges in poetic language. Rooted in the Buddhist notion of impermanence, living on in this transient world is seen as something agonizing. Nagara no hashi, which was repeatedly destroyed by floods throughout history, conjures up an image of fragility, raising the question of how long it will last. This transience of the bridge forms a delicate metaphor for enduring this fleeting, sorrowful world, intertwining the bridge’s transiency with feelings of resignation and melancholy.

field_commentary.value: 「長柄の橋の徒らに」は「橋の板」と言い掛けて「いたずらに」と言葉を続けている。心の目で見える景色として、難波の浦の南側に住吉、東に草香山、北に長柄の橋をあげたあと、西の極楽浄土ではなく、突如盲目の身であることを思い出す。そのきっかけとして長柄の橋が配置されており、度重なる水難により何度架けても「いたずらに」なってしまう長柄の橋という悲劇的な歴史のイメージが関係する。そして、盲目が故に、「いたずらに」雑踏の中を歩いたことで、人とぶつかり笑われて絶望する姿に接続する。

field_commentary_eng.value: The phrase "Nagara no hashi no itazura ni" (the futility of Nagara bridge) takes up the bridge planks (ita) as a pivot word. In the scene envisioned through Shuntokumaru’s mind’s eye, he recalls the view of Sumiyoshi to the south of Naniwa Bay, Mount Kusaka to the east, and Nagara Bridge to the north. Yet, rather than seeing the Pure Land in the West, he suddenly remembers his blindness. The presence of Nagara Bridge here brings its tragic history to mind, constantly swept away by floods no matter how many times it was rebuilt, reflecting the futility implied by "itazura ni". This also parallels Shuntokumaru’s blind condition, since he is walking aimlessly, colliding with others, is mocked, and sinks into despair.

field_scene_description.value: 能《弱法師》の舞台である四天王寺では、鳥居越しに見る夕日が、極楽浄土のある西の方向に沈んで見えることから、極楽浄土を心に感じるために、夕日を見る日想観が流行した。この場面は、日想観のために多くの人が夕日を眺める中、俊徳丸（シテ）も盲目の目で夕日を見つめ、心の目で目前の美しい景色が見えると言い、昔、見慣れた難波江周辺の景色を謡う。弱法師こと俊徳丸は、盲目ではあるが清々しい心境で心で見える景色を詠みあげるが、雑踏のなかで次第に盲目の身であることを思い出し、段々物狂おしくなる様子が描かれる。

field_scene_description_eng.value: At Shitennōji Temple, which is the setting of the play, the sun sets in the West, precisely in the direction associated with the Pure Land paradise. The sight of the sunset through the torii gate thus became a popular way for people to feel a sense of the Pure Land in their hearts. Amidst those watching the sunset, Shuntokumaru (shite) also gazes at it with his blind eyes, saying that he can see the beautiful scene before him through his mind’s eye in this scene. He praises the familiar landscapes around Naniwa Bay that he once knew well. Although blind, Shuntokumaru describes the scenery he envisions with a calm and clear spirit. Gradually, however, he recalls his own blindness, and his mood becomes increasingly distressed, spiraling into a sense of madness.

field_commentary.value: 「君が代が長く続く」と言いかけて、「長柄の橋」を掛け、『古今集』1051番、伊勢の歌「難波なる長柄の橋も造るなり今はわが身を何にたとへむ」を引く。この和歌は古くからある長柄の橋が新たに造りかえられたことを歌っており、謡曲では、新しい時代の到来を予感させる一セイとして機能している。シテの王仁は、日本朝廷に仕えた百済国の学者と伝承され、難波津の歌で仁徳天皇の即位を祝った。能《難波》では、新しい為政者の誕生を春に例えて祝う祝意が込められている。

field_commentary_eng.value: As he begins to say, Nagara no hashi (Nagara Bridge), he plays on the word nagarau (endure), meaning “May your reign endure,” and connects it to poem number 1051 from the Kokinwakashū, attributed to Ise:  “Nagara no hashi in Naniwa is being rebuilt anew — Now, to what might I compare myself?” This waka reflects the reconstruction of the ancient Nagara Bridge and subtly hints at the dawn of a new era. Wani, the shite, is a legendary figure known as a scholar from the kingdom of Baekje who served the Japanese court. He is famously credited with celebrating Emperor Nintoku's accession with a poem about the port of Naniwa. In the Nō play Naniwa, the birth of a new ruler is delicately celebrated and metaphorically linked to the arrival of spring.

field_scene_description.value: 中国から日本の智恵を計ろうとしてやってきた白楽天（ワキ）が、漁翁（シテ）と漁夫（ツレ）と出会う場面。白楽天が名乗る前から漁翁たちが、白楽天だと言い当てたので、白楽天がなぜ分かったのかという問いに対しての漁翁・漁夫の返事に、日本の智慧を計るためにやってくると聞き、毎日船を見るたびに待っていたという意味で「松浦舟」が用いられる。

field_context.value: シテ詞「これこそ二本の杉にて候へよくよく御覧候へ。 ワキ詞「さては二本の杉にて候ひけるぞや。二本の杉の立所を尋ねずは。詞古川の辺に君を見ましやとは。何とよまれたる古歌にて候ふぞ。 シテ「是は光る源氏のいにしへ。玉葛の内侍この初瀬に詣で給ひしを。右近とかや見奉りてよみし歌なり。共にあはれと思しめして御あとをよく弔ひ給ひ候へ。 地クリ｢げにや有りし世をなほ夕顔の露の身の。消えにしあとはなかなかに何なでしこの形見も憂し。 シテサシ｢あはれ思ひの玉葛。かけてもいさや知らざりし。 地｢心尽し木の間の月。雲井のよそにいつしかと。鄙の住居の憂きのみか。さてしもたえてあるべき身を。 シテ｢猶しをりつる人心の。地｢あらき浪風立ち隔て。 クセ｢たよりとなれば早舟に乗りおくれじと松浦がた。唐土船を慕ひしに。心ぞかはる我はただ。浮島を。漕ぎ離れても行く方や何く泊りと白波に。響の灘も過ぎ。思ひに障る方もなし。かくて都の内とても。われは浮きたる舟のうち。なほや憂き目を水鳥の陸にまどへる。心地してたづきも知らぬ身の程を。思ひ歎きて行き悩む。足曳の大和路や。唐土までも聞ゆなる。初瀬の寺に詣でつつ。

field_commentary_eng.value: "Seki no to sasade" is a proverbial expression symbolizing peace. It means that the gate of the Ōsaka barrier, which protects Kyōto from the barbarians of the eastern provinces, is not closed. In other words, it signifies that the world is peaceful due to righteous governance.

field_commentary.value: 坂上田村麻呂は「普天の下。卒土の内いづく王地にあらざるや。（天が下に天皇の土地でないところなどあるはずはない）」と、東国の夷狄を平らげるため遠征する。都を出でて閉ざされていない逢坂の関を越えればそこは近江、石山寺の観音は清水寺の観音と同じ利益があるという。石山寺の前には琵琶湖にかかる瀬田の唐橋。古来この橋が東国の敵との攻防の要となっていた。この橋もやすやすと越えて、東へ向かう田村麻呂の勇ましさを描写する。

field_commentary_eng.value: Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, in his campaign to quell the eastern barbarians, declares, "Under heaven, which place in the land of the Emperor would be no royal territory?" This reflects his resolve as he embarks on his expedition. Leaving the capital and crossing the Ōsaka barrier, which remains open, he enters the province of Ōmi. He reaches Ishiyama-dera whose Kannon (the goddess of mercy) is believed to offer the same blessings as Kiyomizu-dera in Kyōto. In front of Ishiyama-dera lies the Seta no karahashi, a bridge spanning Lake Biwa. Since ancient times, this bridge has been a strategic point in the defense against enemies from the eastern provinces. With ease, Tamuramaro crosses this bridge, further illustrating his courage as he heads eastward.

This reflects his resolve as he embarks on his expedition. Leaving the capital and crossing the Ōsaka barrier, which remains open, he enters the province of Ōmi. He reaches Ishiyama-dera whose Kannon (the goddess of mercy) is believed to offer the same blessings as Kiyomizu-dera in Kyōto. In front of Ishiyama-dera lies the Seta no karahashi, a bridge spanning Lake Biwa. Since ancient times, this bridge has been a strategic point in the defense against enemies from the eastern provinces. With ease, Tamuramaro crosses this bridge, further illustrating his courage as he heads eastward.

Reflecting the sentiment of Sei Shōnagon’s poem, "Try if you wish / to fool others with rooster calls / in the depths of night ̶  / but still closed to your passage / will be the gate at Meeting Hill" (Goshūi wakashū, Miscellaneous II; transl. Steven Carter), the Ōsaka barrier is renowned for its strict vigilance. However, Kumano’s feelings of urgency and anticipation are vividly expressed as she resolves to avoid being stopped at the barrier and hastens to return to her ill mother in the eastern provinces.

field_commentary.value: 『関寺小町』は逢坂の関周辺に住んでいる小野小町の老年の姿を描く能であるが、ここで描かれる小町はときに狷介で、冷笑的である。「逢坂」は「仏法に逢う」を引き出す縁語としても用いられる。「逢坂の山風の。是生滅法の理をも得ばこそ。」とは、ここ逢坂の地に住んで仏法に逢い「是生滅法（生ある者は必ず滅びる）」という教えを得ているはずであるのに、自分はそういったありがたい教えも心から肯うことはできない、という自嘲であり、またこの老女が人間は悟りきれるものではないという虚無的な考えをもっていることをあらわす。老女は「飛花落葉のをりをり」に「好ける道」すなわち和歌の道にいそしみながら老いさらばえていくのだ、という。

field_commentary_eng.value:
Sekidera Komachi is a Nō play that portrays the elderly Ono no Komachi living near the Ōsaka barrier. The Komachi depicted here is sometimes portrayed as reclusive and cynically detached. The word "Ōsaka (written Ausaka)" serves as a pivot word, evoking "meeting (au) the Buddhist teachings." The line, "The mountain wind at Ōsaka. If only I could truly grasp the principle of 'all conditioned phenomena being transient,'" reflects her self-deprecating acknowledgment. While living at Ōsaka barrier, she ought to have embraced the Buddhist truth of shōmetsuhō ("all things that are born must eventually perish"), yet she admits she cannot fully internalize such profound teachings. This suggests the old woman’s nihilistic belief that human beings cannot completely attain enlightenment.
The old woman also expresses that, "In the moments of falling blossoms and scattering leaves," she continues to engage in "the beloved path," referring to the art of waka poetry, even as she declines into old age.

field_commentary_eng.value:
At the eastern edge of the capital, on mount Ōsaka, a decree is issued to abandon Prince Semimaru—a figure considered ominous to the Emperor. The retainers obediently carry out this decision. Prince Semimaru, exiled by his father to the remote region of Mount Ōsaka, experiences profound despair and anxiety, captured through the imagery of "twisting a single thread" (kataito o yoru), which leads to the expression (yorube nashi) being "without support or refuge". This metaphor not only conveys his isolation but also evokes the idea of "twisting threads together," symbolizing the concept of "meeting" (au), which ties into the significance of the barrier Ōsaka (Ōsaka no seki).
The analogy of the blind turtle and floating log is also invoked to deepen this expression. It refers to the nearly impossible chance of a blind turtle in the vast ocean encountering a piece of wood with a hole that perfectly fits its neck. This metaphor, rooted in Buddhist teachings, illustrates how rare and precious it is for a person to encounter Buddha’s teachings in this world. Semimaru’s blindness reflects his uncertain state, and his doubts about whether he can truly encounter and embrace Buddhist teachings while living in exile at Mount Ōsaka mirror this existential uncertainty.

field_scene_description_eng.value: At the beginning of the play, the imperial envoy Kiyotsura (waki) and two palanquin bearers (waki-tsure) arrive at Mount Ōsaka to abandon Prince Semimaru (tsure). The story of Semimaru, a blind man of Ōsaka, is recorded in Konjaku Monogatari and The Tale of the Heike. While Semimaru is not necessarily a prince, in this play, he is portrayed as the fourth son of Emperor Engi. The waki and wakizure, who have come to secretly abandon the prince, sing about their reluctance to move forward, deeply moved by Semimaru’s tragic fate.

field_commentary.value: 父帝に辺境の地である逢坂山に追いやられる皇子蝉丸の絶望と不安を「 片糸をよる」から「よるべなし」を引き出して描写している。また「片糸をよりあわせる」から「あう」のイメージを呼び出し、逢坂山につなぐ。盲亀浮木のたとえは目の見えない亀が、大海原で自分の首の太さと同じ大きさの穴があいた木片に出逢い、その穴に首を突っ込むほどのありえないほど稀な確率をいい、人間がこの世で仏教に出逢うのはこのような確率と同じなのだから、非常に「有難い」ことだという意味で、蝉丸の目の見えない境涯と、逢坂山で出家してほんとうに仏教の教えにであうことができるのだろうかという不安を表現している。

field_commentary.value: 「彼の遍照がよみし杖」とは、「ちはやぶる神やきりけむつくからに千とせの坂もこえぬべらなり（古今348）」という遍照の和歌による。この和歌は光孝天皇の親王時代、天皇の伯母が八十歳の祝いに賜った白銀の杖を詠んだもの。「つくからに」は「神が憑く」と「杖をつく」を懸けた。遍照が詠んだ杖は「千歳の栄」の杖であるが、ここ逢坂山では藁屋の支えであるなあ、という詠嘆。

field_commentary_eng.value:
"The staff Henjō composed a poem about" refers to the following waka:
"The awe-inspiring gods must have carved it? If you lean on this staff you will surely reach the steep slope of a thousand years (of age)." (Kokin wakashū 348).
This poem was written on the occasion when Emperor Kōkō, while still a prince, presented his eighty-year-old aunt with a silver staff in celebration of her long life. The phrase "tsuku kara ni" cleverly plays on the dual meanings of "to lean on a staff" and "to be possessed by a deity" (kami ga tsuku).
While the staff in Henjō's poem symbolizes "a thousand years of prosperity," in the context of Mount Ōsaka, it becomes a poignant expression for the support in a humble straw hut. The unjust and painful reality of Semimaru's life is expressed through the phrase, "In such a sorrowful world, at Ōsaka" (kakaru ukiyo ni Ōsaka no), which reflects his plight. This reference to mount Ōsaka is then connected to Semimaru’s famous waka:
"Here it is: the gate / where people coming and going / must part company, / where both friends and strangers meet ̶ / on the slopes of Meeting Hill" (Gosen wakashū 1089, transl. Steven Carter).
Drawing on this, the phrase, “Whether known or unknown, behold this!” (shiru mo shiranu mo kore miyo ya) follows.
The notion of Semimaru being an "imperial prince of the Engi era" (i.e., a son of Emperor Daigo) stems from a passage in "The Tale of the Heike" (Heike Monogatari, Kakuichibon text), in the section "Volume 10: The Journey Down the Eastern Sea Road."

Left behind, Semimaru holds onto the biwa, the staff, and the few possessions that accompany him, and collapses in tears. In the first half of the play, through the exchange between Kiyotsura (waki) and Semimaru (shite), the chorus (jiutai) chants about Semimaru's harsh circumstances.

field_commentary.value: 憂き世の不条理に逢う蝉丸の境遇を「かかる憂き世に逢坂の」と謡い、さらにその「逢坂山」から「これやこの行くも帰るも別れつつ知るも知らぬもあふさかの関（後撰集1089）」という蝉丸の和歌を引き出し、「知るも知らぬもこれ見よや。」という。なお、蝉丸を「延喜の皇子」すなわち醍醐天皇の皇子とするのは『平家物語（覚一本）』「巻十 海道下り」における記述から。

field_commentary.value: 蝉丸の姉妹である皇女逆髪が登場し、見た目は髪の逆立った狂女だが、心は清いと謡い、「関の清水」につなぐ。「逢坂の関の清水に影見えて今や引くらん望月の駒（拾遺集）」は紀貫之の和歌。「影見ゆ」は「望月」の縁語。また望月は信濃国の地名で、この地から朝廷に馬を奉献した。仲秋十五夜に馬を索いて逢坂山を越えるイメージ。

field_commentary_eng.value:
Semimaru’s sister, the imperial princess Sakagami (Reversed Hair), appears as a crazed woman with disheveled, upstanding hair, yet it is sung that her heart is pure. This connects to "seki no shimizu" ("the pure water of the barrier").
The poem,
"On the surface of the pure water of Ōsaka Barrier, a reflection appears —Now at full moon must they be passing with the horses (from Shinano to the capital)" (Shūi wakashū, 170), is attributed to Ki no Tsurayuki.
The phrase "reflection appears" is a poetic association (engo, linked word) with "full moon" (mochizuki). Additionally, "mochizuki" refers to a place name in Shinano province (modern-day Nagano prefecture), from which horses were offered to the imperial court. This evokes an image of crossing Mount Ōsaka in search of horses on the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival (the fifteenth night of the eighth lunar month).

field_commentary_eng.value:
The phrase "to say one’s name" (na wo iu) evokes the term "ifutsuge-dori" (the yūtsuge-dori or "evening-telling bird"). This bird, associated with Ōsaka barrier as an engo (linking word), appears in numerous waka, such as:
"does the beribboned / cock of Meeting Hill share my / unfulfilled longings ̶ / is it for love alone that / we raise our solemn voices"
(Kokin wakashū 536, transl. Rodd, Henkenius).
This poetic connection is further extended to "tears that cannot be held back at the barrier of Ōsaka" (Ōsaka no sekiaenu namida), creating a poignant image of overflowing emotions that resonate with the sorrow of parting and longing.

field_commentary_eng.value:
The hope of someday being reunited with her husband is expressed through the phrase "mata itsuka Ōsaka no" ("someday again at Ōsaka"). The following term, "yūtsukedori" (evening-telling bird), is an engo (associated word) for Ōsaka.
Many poems use both Ōsaka and yūtsukedori together, such as this one from the Kokin wakashū (no. 634, author unknown):
"I have yearned so long / and at last tonight we meet ̶ / may the beribboned / cock at Ōsaka never / announce the break of day" (transl. Rodd, Henkenius)

field_commentary_eng.value:
This is a famous waka by Semimaru, in the Gosen wakashū (no. 1089)
"Here it is: the gate / where people coming and going / must part company, / where both friends and strangers meet ̶ / on the slopes of Meeting Hill" (transl. Steven Carter)
This poem was also included in the Hyakunin isshu. In the context of the play, it reflects the journey (michiyuki) of Morihisa to his inevitable fate, having been exiled to the east. The line, "Passing through the forest of Oiso, onward to Mino, Owari (which is homophonic to mi no owari, the end of ones life)," expresses Morihisa’s deep awareness that as he continues eastward, he is heading toward the end of his life, a realization woven into the song.

field_commentary.value: 「かかる奇特に逢坂の」と、住吉の神の恵みに逢ったことをよろこび、逢坂の関の傍らに湧く「関の清水に」につなぐ。これは、貫之の「逢坂の関の清水に影見えて今や引くらん望月の駒（拾遺集）」の和歌を呼び起こす。この歌で天皇に献上される「望月の駒」（信濃望月地方の馬、また月毛の馬）を思い起こさせ、能のはじめで貫之の乗ってきた馬のイメージを提示するのである。その馬が蟻通神社の門前でうごけなくなったのを、和歌の神である住吉明神の奇瑞によって、もとどおりに歩めるようなったと喜び、これは和歌の力であると謡う。

field_commentary_eng.value:
The phrase "kakaru kitoku ni Ōsaka no" ("such a wondrous blessing at Ōsaka") conveys the joy of receiving the grace of the Sumiyoshi deity. This joy is linked to "seki no shimizu ni" ("the pure water of the barrier"), calling to mind Tsurayuki's waka:
"On the surface of the pure water of Ōsaka Barrier, a reflection appears —Now at full moon must they be passing with the horses (from Shinano to the capital)" (Shūi wakashū, 170).
This poem evokes the "horse of the full moon" (mochizuki no koma), a horse either from the Mochizuki region of Shinano province or a pale moon-colored horse, offered to the emperor. The imagery of this horse is introduced at the beginning of the play as the one Tsurayuki had ridden.
The narrative celebrates the miraculous event when this horse, having become unable to move on at the gate of the Aritoshi shrine, was restored to its ability to walk through the divine power of Sumiyoshi Myōjin, the god of poetry. This moment is interpreted as a testament to the power of waka poetry and is sung in praise.

The phrase "kakaru kitoku ni Ōsaka no" ("such a wondrous blessing at Ōsaka") conveys the joy of receiving the grace of the Sumiyoshi deity. This joy is linked to "seki no shimizu ni" ("the pure water of the barrier"), calling to mind Tsurayuki's waka:
"On the surface of the pure water of Ōsaka Barrier, a reflection appears —Now at full moon must they be passing with the horses (from Shinano to the capital)" (Shūi wakashū, 170).
This poem evokes the "horse of the full moon" (mochizuki no koma), a horse either from the Mochizuki region of Shinano province or a pale moon-colored horse, offered to the emperor. The imagery of this horse is introduced at the beginning of the play as the one Tsurayuki had ridden.
The narrative celebrates the miraculous event when this horse, having become unable to move on at the gate of the Aritoshi shrine, was restored to its ability to walk through the divine power of Sumiyoshi Myōjin, the god of poetry. This moment is interpreted as a testament to the power of waka poetry and is sung in praise.

field_commentary.value: 能『融』の名所教えの部分。六条河原から東をみて、音羽山の程近くに逢坂の関があるというが、教えられる僧は、音羽山に隠れて見えないという。藤原元方の「音羽山おとに聞きつつ逢坂の関のこなたに年を経ふるかな（古今473）」に拠った詞章。ただし元方は関の東側に住んで音羽山のことは噂に聞いているが、見ることができない、と歌っているのに対し、この能では、見えているのは音羽山で、その向こうにある逢坂の関は見えないと言っている。

field_commentary_eng.value: This is the scene in the play Tōru, where a famous place is described. Looking east from Rokujō Kawara, it is said that Ōsaka barrier is near Mount Otowa. However, the monk who is being taught in this scene says that Mount Otowa hides the view of the barrier. This passage is based on the poem by Fujiwara no Motokata: "I hear rumors of / her borne by Mount Sound of Wings / and yet here on the / far side of Meeting Hill I / pass the years in barren dreams" (Kokin wakashū 473, transl. Rodd, Henkenius). In Motokata's poem, the lyrical I lives on the eastern side of the barrier and knows Mount Otowa from rumors, but he cannot see it. In contrast, in this play, it is Mount Otowa that is in sight, but the barrier beyond it cannot be seen.

field_commentary_eng.value:
A monk setting out on a pilgrimage to the eastern provinces chants a travel song (michiyuki). Referring to the capital as "karaku" (Flower Capital) in classical Chinese is extremely rare, appearing only three times across the entire Collection of 350 Nō plays. In contrast, the expression "hana no miyako" (blooming capital) is used 49 times, making the former overwhelmingly less common.
In this case, it is thought that the term "karaku" was chosen as it was a word likely used by the monks of the Five Great Temples (Gozan), who were well-versed in Chinese poetry.

The phrase "at the pure water of the Barrier, a reflection appears" serves as a prelude to mount Ōsaka, and it derives from Ki no Tsurayuki’s poem: "On the surface of the pure water of Ōsaka Barrier, a reflection appears —Now at full moon must they be passing with the horses (from Shinano to the capital)" (Shūi wakashū, 170).

field_commentary_eng.value:
Ōwada Tateki's Yōkyoku hyōshaku references the Kokin eigashō and includes an explanation of the "Festival of the four barriers" (Shikyō no sai). It states:
"Attaching paper streamers to chicken, and having onmyōji (masters of yin and yang divination) pray to dispel ill fortune. The birds are then released at the four borders of the land, and these are called yūtsukedori. The four borders are as follows: in the east, Ōsaka; in the north, Aruchi; in the south, Tatsuta; and in the west, Anao."
In this particular piece, Tatsuta is the setting, but there is also mention of Ōsaka, one of the "Four barriers."

field_commentary.value: 逢坂の関を越え琵琶湖畔に出でれば松本、打出浜。この近辺は江戸初期に選出されたとされる近江八景のひとつ「粟津晴嵐」の地。「晴嵐」は松林に風が吹くさまを形容するが、謡曲成立時も松本近辺は「嵐」のイメージがあったか。そこから同じく近江八景「矢橋帰帆」に謡いつぐ。矢橋は琵琶湖の東岸であり、舟で琵琶湖を渡って東国に向かう経路である。

field_commentary_eng.value: Crossing the Ōsaka barrier and emerging on the shores of Lake Biwa, one arrives at Matsumoto and Uchidehama. This area is the site of Awazu no seiran ("clear breeze at Awazu"), one of the Eight Views of Ōmi (Ōmi hakkei), which were selected in the early Edo period. The term seiran (clear breeze) describes the wind blowing through pine groves, and it seems that even at the time when nō plays were being written, the area around Matsumoto was associated with the image of a storm. From there, the narrative transitions to Yabase kihan ("Returning sails at Yabase"), another of the Eight Views of Ōmi. Yabase, located on the eastern shore of Lake Biwa, was part of the route for crossing the lake by boat and traveling onward to the eastern provinces (Tōgoku).

field_commentary.value:
六代御とは平維盛の嫡子、平高清のこと。斎藤五と斎藤六は兄弟であり、高清の傅人(付き添って世話をする人)であった。『平家物語』『六代御前物語』に類似の話が見られることから、このどちらか、あるいは双方に取材したものか。
 「逢坂」は都から鎌倉に向かう道中の地名だが、「いつ迄このような辛い世に迷い続けたらよいのだろうか、今、六代との別れ路に遭遇して逢阪の関を越えて鎌倉に向かっている」という文脈で、六代と死別するかもしれない運命との遭遇とを嘆く掛け詞となっている。

「逢坂」は都から鎌倉に向かう道中の地名だが、「いつ迄このような辛い世に迷い続けたらよいのだろうか、今、六代との別れ路に遭遇して逢阪の関を越えて鎌倉に向かっている」という文脈で、六代と死別するかもしれない運命との遭遇とを嘆く掛け詞となっている。

field_commentary_eng.value:
"Rokudai gozen" refers to Taira no Takakiyo, the eldest son of Taira no Koremori. Saitō Go and Saitō Roku were brothers and served as Takakiyo's attendants, responsible for looking after him. Similar stories can be found in The Tale of the Heike and The Tale of Rokudai gozen, suggesting that this play may have drawn from one or both of these sources.
"Ōsaka" is a place name along the road from the capital (Kyōto) to Kamakura. In this context, it is used as a poetic pivot to express lament: "How much longer must I wander in this cruel world? Now, at this crossroads of parting from Rokudai, I cross the barrier at Ōsaka and head toward Kamakura." Here, the word "Ōsaka" conveys both the physical journey and an emotional encounter with the fate of possibly parting from Rokudai in death.

「誰かいひし春の色は」は、『和漢朗詠集』菅原文時の詩句「誰言春色從レ東到、霞暖南枝花始開。」を引いた。
 木花開耶姫は、本曲の後ヅレ。記紀などに見える神。大山祇神（おおやまつみのかみ）の娘。磐長姫（いわながひめ）の妹。美しい容姿を天孫瓊瓊杵尊（ににぎのみこと）に好まれてその妃となり、火酢芹命（ほのすせりのみこと）、火明命（ほのあかりのみこと）、彦火火出見尊（ひこほほでみのみこと）を生む。（『日本国語大辞典』）

field_commentary.value:
難波の鐘も響きはじめたが、その鐘の音も、浦にうち寄せる波の声も、入江の松風も、村芦の葉音も、皆悦びの声を揃え、しかも諫鼓を打つ音に鳥の驚かされることはない、誠に太平の御盛代だ。
 諫鼓とは天子を諫る鼓である。「諫鼓苔むし」は、『和漢朗詠集』大江音人の詩句「刑鞭蒲朽螢空去、諫鼓苔深鳥不レ驚」から引いた。天下がよく治まり訴訟する者もなかったので無用のものとなり自然に苔が生えたという。太平のしるしである。

難波は入江に近いということか、「入江の水を引き入れるのは難波の田」と歌われている。「ふし水」は流れない溜水のことを指す。
 古例は未確認だが、室町末期の御伽草子『猿源氏草紙』などに「一とせなにはいり江に、橋の供養ありし時」とあって、「難波江」とほぼ同じ意味で「難波入江」の用例があり、この謡曲にも影響したか。

field_context.value:
物着地クリ「それたかき山ふかき海。妹背恋路の跡ながら。ことに難波の海山の。処からなる情とかや。
 シテサシ「あるは男山の昔を思ひ出でて。
 地「女郎花の一時をくねると云へども。いひ慰むる言の葉の。露もたわわに秋萩の。本の契の消えかへり。つれなかりける命かな。
 シテ「さればかほどに衰へて。
 地「身を羽束師の森なれども。
 言葉の花こそ便なれ。
 クセ「難波津に。さくやこの花冬ごもり。今は春べと咲くや。この花と栄え給ひける。仁徳天皇と。聞えさせ給ひしは難波の御子の御事。又浅香山の言の葉は。采女の。盃とりあへぬ。恨をのべし故とかや。此二歌は今までの。歌の父母なる故に。代々にあまねき花色の。言の葉草の種とりて。我等如きの手習ふ初なるべし。然れば目に見えぬ鬼神をもやはらげ。武士の心なぐさむる。夫婦の情知る事も今身の上に知られたり。
 シテ「津の国の。難波の春は夢なれや。
 地「芦の枯葉に風渡る。波の立居のひまとても浅かるべしやわたづみの。浜の真砂は。よみ尽し尽すとも。此道は尽きせめや。唯玩べ名にしおふ。なにはの恨うち忘れて。ありし契に帰りあふ縁こそ嬉しかりけれ。

field_commentary.value: ここでの「難波」は『菟玖波集』におさめられた連歌「草の名もところによりて変るなり」「難波の芦は伊勢の濱荻」を踏まえた表現。また、『嘉応二年十月九日住吉社歌合』藤原俊成の跋に「この神風伊勢島には浜荻と名づくれど、難波わたりにはあしとのみいひ、吾妻の方にはよし問ふなるが如くに」とあり、同じ草を浜荻とも「あし」とも「よし」ともいうことを記す。ここでは、伊勢の神子であるが難波人のことも分かるという意味であり、さらに難波を「なには」にいいかけ、「いかなることでも」という意味の掛詞としている。

field_commentary.value: このクリ・サシ・クセは、『古今和歌集』仮名序を踏まえている。「難波津の歌はみかどのおほんはじめなり、浅香山の言葉は采女の戯れより詠みて、この二歌は歌の父母のやうにてぞ手習ふ人の始にもしける」とあり、古注によると、ここで取り上げた二つの和歌は、それぞれに、「難波津にさくやこの花冬ごもり今は春べと咲やこの花」「浅香山影さへ見ゆる山の井の浅き心をわが主はなくに」の歌を指す。『謡曲評釈』「芳野」の注によると、ここで貫之がこの二つの歌を取り上げるのは、「歌道ははじめは浅はかなるようなれど、入れば入るほど奥の深きをいへり」という道理を語るためであろう、とする。

field_commentary.value: 「富士のなるさの大将」は、鴨長明『無明抄』を基にした表現。徳大寺実定が「無明の酒」を「名もなき酒」と詠み誤ったことで、「名なしの大将」と呼ばれ、藤原俊成が「富士のなるさは（鳴沢）」を「富士のなるさ」と詠み誤ったことで、「富士のなるさの入道」という不名誉なあだ名を付けられた話を踏まえたもの。「富士のなるさの入道」と「名なしの大将」を合わせて「富士のなるさの大将」としたものか。続く「四病八病」は和歌を作る際のよくある誤りを挙げた「歌病」のこと。「三代八部同じ文字」は、鎌倉時代までの勅撰和歌集である三代集（『古今集』『後撰集』『拾遺集』）や八部集（三代集に『後拾遺集』『金葉集』『詞花集』『千載集』『新古今集』を加えたもの）の和歌と同じ文字を使う意味で、いずれも和歌を詠む上での誤りを示す言葉である。

 貫之「御前に候。
 王「始より小町が相手には黒主を定めたり。まづまづ小町が歌を読み上げ候へ。
 貫之「畏つて候。水辺の草。蒔かなくに何を種とて浮草の。波のうねうね生ひ茂るらん。
 王「面白とよみたる歌や。此歌に優るはよもあらじ。皆々詠じ候へ。
 貫之「畏つて候。
 ワキ「暫く候。これは古歌にて候。
 王「何と古歌と申すか。
 ワキ「さん候。
 王「いかに小町。何とて古歌をば申すぞ。
 シテ「恥かしの勅諚やな。先代の昔はそも知らず。既に衣通姫此道のすたらん事を歎き。和歌の浦曲に跡を垂れ給ひ。玉津島の明神より此方。皆此道をたしなむなり。それに今の歌を古歌と仰せ候ふは。古今万葉の勅撰にて候ふか。又は家の集にてあるやらん。作者は誰にてましますぞ。委しく仰せ候へ。
 ワキ詞「仰の如く其証歌分明ならではいかでか奏し申すべき。草子は万葉題は夏。水辺の草とは見えたれども。読人しらずとかきたれば。作者は誰とも存ぜぬなり。
 シテ「それ万葉は奈良の御宇。撰者は橘の諸兄。歌の数は七千首に及んで。皆わらはが知らぬ歌はさむらはず。万葉といふ草子に数多の本の候ふかおぼつかなうこそ候へ。
 ワキ「げにげにそれはさる事なれどもさりながら。御身は衣通姫の流なれば。憐む歌にて強からねば。古歌を盗むは道理なり。
 シテ「さては御事は古の猿丸太夫のながれ。それは猿猴の名をもつて。我が名をよそに立てんとや。正しくそれは古歌ならず。
 ワキ「花の蔭行く山賎の。
 シテ「その様賎しき身ならねば。何とて古歌とは見るべきぞ。
 ワキ「さて詞をたださで誤りしは。富士のなるさの大将や。四病八病三代八部同じ文字。
 シテ「もじもかほどの誤は。
 ワキ「昔も今も。
 シテ「ありぬべし。
 地「不思議や上古も末代も。三十一字のそのうちに。一字もかはらで詠みたる歌。これ万葉の歌ならば。和歌の不思議と思ふべし。さらば証歌をいだせとの。宣旨度々下りしかば。初は立春の題なれば。花も尽きぬと引き開く。夏は涼しき浮草の。これこそ今の歌なりとて。既に読まんとさし上ぐれば。我が身に当らぬ歌人さへ。胸に苦しき手を置けり。ましてや小町が心のうち、唯轟きの橋うち渡りて。危き心は隙もなし。

field_commentary.value: この「富士」は、相手の「浅間」とともに、楽人の名前であって、山の名ではないが、『後撰集』の和歌「信濃なる浅間の山も燃ゆなれば富士の煙のかひやなからん」（謡曲本文では小異あり）を踏まえたもの。その意味で「富士浅間いづれも面白き名なり」と言い、「名こそ上なき富士」というのも、「名に使われている富士山は、日本で最も高い山ではあるが」という意味。

field_commentary.value: 「それは越路に帰る山これは名高き富士の嶺の」は、『古今集』に「越へまかりける人によみてつかはしける」として載る紀利貞の和歌「かへる山ありとは聞けど春霞立ち別れなば恋しかるべし」などに詠まれる「帰山」である。古くから多くの歌や紀行文にみえるが、その位置については諸説あって定かでない（『日本歴史地名大系』）。「かりがね」が謡われるのは、中国前漢の蘇武が、匈奴に捕虜となった後も、雁の足に書を結び付けて手紙のやりとりをした故事を踏まえ、その雁が「かえる」と山と言えば、越路にある帰山があるが、鬼王・団三郎が帰って来たのは、その帰る山ではなくて、富士山の麓からだ、の意味。

field_commentary.value: 「三笠の森」は、辞典類には福岡県大野城市の「御笠の森」ばかりが立項されるが、《佐保山》は奈良を舞台とした演目であり、春日大社のご神体である奈良県東部の三笠山の森を指すと考えられる。佐保山の東に位置する三笠山は、前のシテ謡の最後「春日野の」から続く「春日野の三笠の森」として自然に接続され、東から昇る月の光が森に差し込む情景を描いている。さらに、天女の来迎を告げる花が舞い落ちることで、幻想的な雰囲気となる。

field_commentary.value:
この《要石》の舞台は常陸国鹿島社（現在の鹿島神宮）であり、ここで使われる「三笠山」は、奈良の春日にある三笠山ではなく、鹿島社が鎮座する山の意味である。
鎌倉時代末期の成立とされる『鹿島宮社例伝記』（『続群書類従』『神道大系 香取・鹿島』所収）に「又御笠大明神トモ云。（中略）春日御笠山之名通ル故カ。〔ウツリ行神ノ宮居ノシルシトヤ爰ヲ御笠ト兼テ云ケン。〕」とあり、春日大社の神霊は、鹿島社から鎮座したとする縁起（国宝『春日権現験記絵』詞書など）に関係させて理解されたらしい。
《要石》作者の徳川斉昭とも関わりがあった国学者・前田夏蔭による「要石謡曲註解」（佐伯有義編『神道叢書』2、1898年、思文閣、1971年復刻所収）でも、三笠山を鹿島社の鎮座地とする。

シテ「此方の事にて候ふか。何事にて候ふぞ。
ワキ「人々は此辺の者にてわたり候ふか。
シテ「さん候この辺に住居する夫婦の海人にて候ふが。日毎に此御神に詣で候へば。また今日も参らばやと存じ。この処に来りて候。まづ御姿を見奉れば。このあたりにては見なれ申さぬ御事なり。そもいづくよりの御参詣にて候ふぞ。

シテ「これこそ高天の浦と申し候へ。

field_context.value:
ワキ詞「如何に是なる女性に尋ね申すべき事の候。
シテ詞「此方の事にて候ふか何事にて候ふぞ。
ワキ「見申せばこれ程茂りたる森林に。重ねて木を植え給ふ事不審にこそ候へ。
シテ「さては当社始めてご参詣の人にて御入り候ふか。
ワキ「さん候始めてこの処に参りて候。当社の謂詳しく御物語り候へ。

シテ「なう其詞はこなたも耳に留るものを。彼の業平も此渡にて。名にしおはば。いざ言問はん都鳥。我が思ふ人は有りやなしやと。
ワキ「あれこそ沖の鴎候ふよ。
シテ「うたてやな浦にては千鳥とも云へ鴎とも云へ。など此隅田川にて白き鳥をば。都鳥とは答へ給はぬ。
ワキ「実に実に誤り申したり。名所には住めども心なくて。都鳥とは答へ申さで。
シテ「沖の鴎とゆふ波の。
ワキ「昔にかへる業平も。
シテ「有りや無しやと言問ひしも。
ワキ「都の人を思妻。
シテ「わらはも東に思子の。ゆくへを問ふは同じ心の。
ワキ「妻をしのび。
シテ「子を尋ぬるも。
ワキ「思は同じ。
シテ「恋路なれば。
地歌「我もまた。いざ言問はん都鳥。いざ言問はん都鳥。我が思子は東路に。有りやなしやと。問へども問へども答へぬはうたて都鳥。鄙の鳥とやいひてまし。実にや舟ぎほふ。堀江の川のみなぎはに。来居つつ鳴くは都鳥。それは難波江これは又隅田川の東まで。思へば限なく。遠くも来ぬるものかな。さりとては渡守。舟こぞりて狭くとも。乗せさせ給へ渡守さりとては乗せてたび給へ。

field_scene_description.value: 子を探す狂女（シテ）は、渡守（ワキ）に狂いの姿を求められると、川面の都鳥を見て、遥かに恋しい相手への思いを、『伊勢物語』に記された在原業平の東下りに重ねて乗船を懇願する場面。
